turns.text: Thanks for joining. Why product management?
I'm finishing an MBA after four years in data engineering. I want to own the why behind what my teams build, not just the how.
Here's the question. How much new storage does Gmail need every day?
Let me clarify a few things. Are we talking about new email data stored per day worldwide, in bytes? And should I include backups or replicas?
New email storage only, worldwide, per day. Ignore redundancy and backup copies unless you want to add them at the end.
Okay. Do we know roughly how many accounts there are?

My approach: daily active users times emails received per user per day times average size per email. And I'll split emails into plain emails and emails with attachments, because attachments dominate size.

Assumptions. Of 1.8 billion accounts, I'd say about 1 billion are active on a given day — lots of accounts are secondary or dormant, maybe half or a bit more are active daily. Each active user receives about 40 emails a day after spam is filtered out — think of newsletters, receipts, notifications, and a few personal emails. Of those 40, I'd guess 10% have an attachment, so 4 emails with attachments and 36 without.
Sizes: a plain email with HTML formatting is around 50 kilobytes. An email with an attachment — PDFs, images — averages maybe 500 kilobytes.

Math: plain emails, 36 times 50 KB is 1,800 KB, call it 1.8 megabytes per user per day. Attachments, 4 times 500 KB is 2,000 KB, 2 megabytes. Total about 3.8 megabytes per user per day. Times 1 billion users is 3.8 billion megabytes, which is 3.8 petabytes per day.
So my answer is roughly 4 petabytes of new storage a day. The assumption that matters most is the attachment share and size — if attachments are 20% instead of 10%, the number goes up by about half.
Okay, thanks. Any questions for me?
How do PMs on storage-heavy products think about cost versus user experience?
